source_paragraphs.quote: 1.1 If $K=\emptyset$, then $W=\emptyset$ and it is compact. Otherwise let $\mathcal V$ be any open cover of $W$. By [F2], $f[K]$ is compact, so [F1] gives finitely many $V_1,\ldots,V_q\in\mathcal V$ covering $f[K]$. Set $O=\bigcup_{i=1}^qV_i$, an open set containing $f[K]$. [given, F1, F2, cases]

2.1 Form the family of all balls $B_Y(y,r)$ with $y\in f[K]$, $r>0$, and $B_Y(y,2r)\subseteq O$. This family covers $f[K]$ by openness and [F3], so [F1] gives a finite subcover with centers $y_1,\ldots,y_s$ and radii $r_1,\ldots,r_s$. Since $f[K]\ne\emptyset$, $s\ge1$; let $\delta=\min_i r_i>0$. If $z\in Y$ and $d_Y(z,y)<\delta$ for some $y\in f[K]$, choose $i$ with $d_Y(y,y_i)<r_i$; then $d_Y(z,y_i)<\delta+r_i\le2r_i$, so $z\in B_Y(y_i,2r_i)\subseteq O$. Thus every point within distance $\delta$ of some point of $f[K]$ lies in $O$. [step 1.1, F1, F3, algebra]

4.1 For each of the finitely many indices $1\le n<N$, [F2] makes $f_n[K]$ compact, so [F1] supplies a finite subfamily of $\mathcal V$ covering it. Together with $V_1,\ldots,V_q$ from step 1.1, these finitely many members cover $f[K]$, all $f_n[K]$ with $n\ge N$, and each remaining $f_n[K]$. Hence every open cover of $W$ has a finite subcover, so $W$ is compact by [F1]. The proof uses only finite subcovers and a finite minimum, not a choice axiom. [step 1.1, step 3.1, F1, F2, algebra] ∎

source_paragraphs.quote: 1.1 Define $\Phi(x,a)=\kappa(x,\cdot)a(\cdot)$ on $\bar D'\times K$. For $(x,a),(x',a')$ in this product, $$\|\Phi(x',a')-\Phi(x,a)\|_\infty\le\|\kappa\|_\infty\|a'-a\|_\infty+\|a\|_\infty\sup_{y\in\bar D}|\kappa(x',y)-\kappa(x,y)|.$$ The constants are finite by [F3]. Given $\eta>0$, uniform continuity of $\kappa$ on $\bar D'\times\bar D$ gives a positive $\delta_1$ making the second term less than $\eta/2$ when $|x'-x|<\delta_1$; choosing $\delta_2>0$ with $\|\kappa\|_\infty\delta_2<\eta/2$ bounds the first term whenever $\|a'-a\|_\infty<\delta_2$ (if $\|\kappa\|_\infty=0$, that term is zero). Thus $\Phi$ is continuous for the max product metric. The domain is compact by [F3], so [F4] makes its image $S$ compact. [given, F3, F4, algebra]
1.2 Put $M=1+\sup_n\|Q_n\|+|D|>0$. For any $f,g\in C(\bar D)$, $$\left|Q_n(f)-\int_Df-Q_n(g)+\int_Dg\right|\le M\|f-g\|_\infty,$$ since $|\int_D(f-g)|\le |D|\|f-g\|_\infty$. [given, F2, algebra]

2.1 Fix $\varepsilon>0$. Put $M=1+\sup_n\|Q_n\|+|D|>0$. By [F1] and step 1.1, choose a finite $\varepsilon/(3M)$-net $f_1,\dots,f_J$ for $S$. For each $j$, [F2] gives an index $n_j$ such that $|Q_n(f_j)-\int_Df_j|<\varepsilon/3$ whenever $n\ge n_j$. [step 1.1, F1, F2, choose]

source_paragraphs.quote: 1.1 Since $U$ is bounded, choose real numbers $a_1<b_1$ with $a_1\le x_1\le b_1$ on $\bar U$. Let $B=\|\widetilde b_1\|_{C^0(U)}$ and $C_0=\|\widetilde c\|_{C^0(U)}$. Choose $\kappa>0$ large enough that $\kappa^2\lambda_0-\kappa B-C_0\ge1$. For $\psi(x)=e^{\kappa x_1}$, [F1] gives $$L[\psi](x)=e^{\kappa x_1}\bigl(\kappa^2a_{11}(x)+\kappa\widetilde b_1(x)+\widetilde c(x)\bigr)\ge e^{\kappa a_1}>0.$$ Choose $M>e^{\kappa b_1}$ and set $\Phi=M-\psi$. Then $\Phi>0$ on $\bar U$ and $L[\Phi]=M\widetilde c-L[\psi]\le-e^{\kappa a_1}$. [given, F1, algebra, choose]

3.1 Suppose $z(x_0)>0$ at some $x_0\in U$. Since $z\le0$ on $\partial U$ and $z$ is continuous on $\bar U$, its positive maximum is attained at an interior point. For sufficiently small $\delta>0$, $z+\delta\psi$ has an interior positive maximum as well: its value at $x_0$ is at least $z(x_0)>0$, while its boundary values are at most $\delta e^{\kappa b_1}<z(x_0)$. At that interior maximum [F2] and $\widetilde c\le0$ give $L[z+\delta\psi]\le0$, contradicting $L[z+\delta\psi]>0$. Hence $z\le0$ on $U$, and therefore $$w\le Q+(R/\eta)\|\Phi\|_{C^0(\bar U)}.$$ Applying the same argument to $-w$ yields the corresponding lower bound. Taking $C_L=\max\{1,\|\Phi\|_{C^0(\bar U)}/\eta\}$ proves the first estimate; applying it to $u^*-h$ proves the second. [step 2.1, F2, algebra] ∎

For $\psi(x)=e^{\kappa x_1}$, [F1] gives $$L[\psi](x)=e^{\kappa x_1}\bigl(\kappa^2a_{11}(x)+\kappa\widetilde b_1(x)+\widetilde c(x)\bigr)\ge e^{\kappa a_1}>0.$$ Choose $M>e^{\kappa b_1}$ and set $\Phi=M-\psi$. Then $\Phi>0$ on $\bar U$ and $L[\Phi]=M\widetilde c-L[\psi]\le-e^{\kappa a_1}$. [given, F1, algebra, choose]

2.1 Put $R=\|L[w]\|_{C^0(U)}$, $Q=\|w\|_{C^0(\partial U)}$, and $\eta=e^{\kappa a_1}$. For $z=w-Q-(R/\eta)\Phi$, the boundary values satisfy $z\le0$. In $U$, $$L[z]=L[w]-Q\widetilde c-(R/\eta)L[\Phi]\ge -R+R=0,$$ because $-Q\widetilde c\ge0$. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Suppose $z(x_0)>0$ at some $x_0\in U$. Since $z\le0$ on $\partial U$ and $z$ is continuous on $\bar U$, its positive maximum is attained at an interior point. For sufficiently small $\delta>0$, $z+\delta\psi$ has an interior positive maximum as well: its value at $x_0$ is at least $z(x_0)>0$, while its boundary values are at most $\delta e^{\kappa b_1}<z(x_0)$. At that interior maximum [F2] and $\widetilde c\le0$ give $L[z+\delta\psi]\le0$, contradicting $L[z+\delta\psi]>0$. Hence $z\le0$ on $U$, and therefore $$w\le Q+(R/\eta)\|\Phi\|_{C^0(\bar U)}.$$ Applying the same argument to $-w$ yields the corresponding lower bound. Taking $C_L=\max\{1,\|\Phi\|_{C^0(\bar U)}/\eta\}$ proves the first estimate; applying it to $u^*-h$ proves the second. [step 2.1, F2, algebra] ∎

source_paragraphs.quote: 1.1 For a fixed horizon $N$, let $\mathcal F_t$ be generated by $\xi_0,\ldots,\xi_{t-1}$, with $\mathcal F_0$ trivial. For every fixed sign prefix of length $t$, exactly half its extensions have $\xi_t=1$ and half have $\xi_t=-1$, so $\mathbb E[\xi_t\mid\mathcal F_t]=0$ and $\operatorname{Var}(\xi_t\mid\mathcal F_t)=1$. Since $x_t$ is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable and $f'(x)=x$, the direction $G_t=x_t+b+\sigma\xi_t$ has conditional mean $x_t+b$ and conditional variance $\sigma^2$; it is unbiased when $b=0$ and has bias $b$ otherwise. All variables have finite moments because the sample space is finite. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F11, given, algebra]

1.2 Put $m_t=\mathbb E[x_t]$. The update is $x_{t+1}=qx_t-\alpha b-\alpha\sigma\xi_t$, hence $m_{t+1}=qm_t-\alpha b$ with $m_0=x_0$. Induction gives $m_t=q^t x_0-b(1-q^t)$ for every $t\le N$. [F1, given, induction, algebra]

2.1 Let $V_t=\mathbb E[(x_t-m_t)^2]$. Because $x_t-m_t$ is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable and $\xi_t$ has conditional mean zero and conditional second moment one, the cross term vanishes and $V_{t+1}=q^2V_t+\alpha^2\sigma^2$, with $V_0=0$. Thus $V_t=\alpha^2\sigma^2\sum_{j=0}^{t-1}q^{2j}=\frac{\alpha\sigma^2}{2-\alpha}(1-q^{2t})$, since $1-q^2=\alpha(2-\alpha)$. Adding $m_t^2$ proves the displayed moment formula, and it is independent of the chosen horizon whenever $N\ge t$. [F2, F4, F11, step 1.2, given, algebra]

2.2 Now assume AC for the published bounds. In the unbiased case, $L=1$, $f_{\inf}=0$, $\Delta=x_0^2/2$, and step 1.1 verifies conditional unbiasedness and variance $\sigma^2$; $\alpha\le1/4\le1/L$. Use [F8] with $p_k=1/N$ and apply [F9] to obtain $\mathbb E|x_{R_N}|^2\le x_0^2/(\alpha N)+\alpha\sigma^2$. [A1, F8, F9, step 1.1, given, algebra]

source_paragraphs.quote: 2.1 For $E=\bigcup_k A_k\times\{k\}$ define $\widetilde P(E)=\sum_k p_kP(A_k)$. This is nonnegative and $\widetilde P(\widetilde\Omega)=\sum_kp_k=1$. If $E_j=\bigcup_k A_{j,k}\times\{k\}$ are pairwise disjoint, then for each fixed $k$ the sets $A_{j,k}$ are pairwise disjoint. Countable additivity of $P$ from [F2] gives $\widetilde P(\bigcup_jE_j)=\sum_kp_k\lim_{m\to\infty}\sum_{j=1}^mP(A_{j,k})$. Because the sum over $k$ is finite, its limit commutes with this finite sum; rearranging each finite double sum gives $\widetilde P(\bigcup_jE_j)=\lim_{m\to\infty}\sum_{j=1}^m\widetilde P(E_j)=\sum_j\widetilde P(E_j)$. Hence $\widetilde P$ is a probability measure. [F1, F2, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 Let $R(\omega,k)=k$. It is measurable because each inverse image is $\Omega\times\{k\}$, and $\widetilde P(R=k)=p_k$. source_paragraphs.quote: 1.1 Fix $t\ge1$ and write $g_t=\nabla f(x_t)$, $m_t=\mathbb E[G_t\mid\mathcal F_t]$, and $\varepsilon_t=G_t-m_t$. The filtration and adapted-process conventions [F3, F4], together with the random-element convention [F5], make the time-indexed measurability explicit. By [F16], the objective values, gradients, and oracle vectors used below are integrable. The vector $\varepsilon_t$ is $\mathcal F_{t+1}$-measurable and has conditional mean zero given $\mathcal F_t$, so each coordinate, after shifting the filtration to $\mathcal H_n=\mathcal F_{n+1}$, is a martingale difference by [F8]. Conditional linearity and order [F11] give $\mathbb E[f(x_{t+1})\mid\mathcal F_t]\le f(x_t)-\alpha_t\langle g_t,m_t\rangle+\frac{L\alpha_t^2}{2}\mathbb E[\|G_t\|_2^2\mid\mathcal F_t]\le f(x_t)-\left(\mu\alpha_t-\frac{LM_G\alpha_t^2}{2}\right)\|g_t\|_2^2+\frac{LM\alpha_t^2}{2}$. All remaining terms are integrable by [F15]–[F16] and the second-moment bound in step 1.1. [A1, A2, A3, A4, F1, F9, F10, F11, F13, F14, F15, F16, step 1.1, algebra]

The objective terms telescope and [A5] gives $\frac{\mu\alpha}{2}\sum_{t=1}^T\mathbb E\|g_t\|_2^2\le f(x_1)-F_{\inf}+\frac{L\alpha^2MT}{2}$. Divide by $T\mu\alpha/2$ to obtain the stated constant-step average bound. [A5, F11, F12, F15, F16, step 2.1, given, algebra]

source_paragraphs.quote: 1.2 At every differentiability point $x\ne0$, differentiating $q(cx)=c^Lq(x)$ with respect to $c$ at $c=1$ gives $\langle x,\nabla q(x)\rangle=Lq(x)$. [given, algebra]

source_paragraphs.quote: 1.1 Strict separability gives $u$ with $m_i(u)>0$ for every $i$. Since the sample is finite, $a:=\min_i m_i(u)>0$. The scaled vector $u/a$ satisfies $m_i(u/a)=m_i(u)/a\ge1$, so the feasible set in [F1] is nonempty. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Put $R=\|u/a\|_2$ and $K=\mathcal F\cap\{w:\|w\|_2\le R\}$. The set $K$ is nonempty by step 1.1 and is closed and bounded by [F1], so [F2] makes it compact and gives a minimizer $w_*$ of $\frac12\|w\|_2^2$ on $K$. Every feasible vector outside the radius-$R$ ball has norm greater than $R$, while $u/a\in K$ has norm $R$; therefore no such vector improves on $w_*$. Hence $w_*$ is a global minimizer on $\mathcal F$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 If two distinct feasible minimizers $w,z$ existed, their midpoint would remain feasible because each $m_i$ is linear. But $\left\|\frac{w+z}{2}\right\|_2^2=\frac12\|w\|_2^2+\frac12\|z\|_2^2-\frac14\|w-z\|_2^2$ is strictly smaller than their common minimum value, a contradiction. Therefore the minimizer is unique. [F1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

Since [F4] and [F7] give $(\log r)'=L\phi\mu/r^2>0$ almost everywhere by step 3.1, absolute continuity makes $r$ strictly increasing; [F5] gives $r\to\infty$. source_paragraphs.quote: 1.1 Write $f(\theta)=\frac12\|\theta\|_2^2$ and $g_i(\theta)=1-q_i(\theta)$. Let $I$ be the finite active set $\{i:q_i(\theta_*)=1\}$. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Set $S:=\partial^\circ f(\theta_*)\cup\bigcup_{i\in I}\partial^\circ g_i(\theta_*)$. Each constituent is compact and convex, so $S$ is bounded. In any finite convex combination of points of $S$, group together the points from each constituent; convexity then writes the combination using at most one point from each of the finitely many constituents. Therefore $C:=\operatorname{conv}(S)$ is the continuous image of the product of those constituents and their finite coefficient simplex. That product is closed and bounded in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, hence compact by [F3], so $C$ is compact, nonempty, and convex. [F1, F3, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 If $0\notin C$, [F4] strictly separates $0$ from $C$, giving a direction $v$ with $\langle h,v\rangle<0$ for every $h\in S$. By [F1], this means $f^\circ(\theta_*;v)<0$ and $g_i^\circ(\theta_*;v)<0$ for every active $i$. The definition of each limsup gives a positive step bound for which each corresponding difference quotient along $\theta_*+tv$ is negative; taking the minimum of these finitely many bounds makes $f(\theta_*+tv)<f(\theta_*)$ and $g_i(\theta_*+tv)<0$ simultaneously for every active constraint. Continuity preserves the already strict inactive constraints. This is a feasible descent from a constrained local minimum, a contradiction. Hence $0\in C$. [F1, F4, step 2.1, given, assume-contra, discharge-contradiction]

4.1 Since $0\in\operatorname{conv}(S)$ and each Clarke subdifferential in $S$ is convex, group the finite convex combination by its constituent set. [F1, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 If there are no active constraints, the coefficients in step 4.1 sum to one, so $\alpha_0=1$. Otherwise, if $\alpha_0=0$, some active coefficient is positive; dotting the equality in step 4.1 with the MFCQ direction from [F2] makes the right-hand sum strictly negative, a contradiction. In either case $\alpha_0>0$. Divide by $\alpha_0$, set $\lambda_i=\alpha_i/\alpha_0$ for active indices and $\lambda_i=0$ otherwise, and put $\widetilde h_i=-h_i\in\partial^\circ q_i(\theta_*)$. source_paragraphs.quote: 1.1 Write $z_h=W_hx_{h-1}$ and $s_1=\sqrt{c_\sigma}$ in both architectures, $s_h=\sqrt{c_\sigma}$ for fully connected $h\ge2$, and $s_h=c_{\rm res}/H$ for residual $h\ge2$. A layer has feature Jacobian $P_h=(s_h/\sqrt m)\operatorname{diag}(\sigma'(z_h))W_h$ in the fully connected case, and $P_h=I+(s_h/\sqrt m)\operatorname{diag}(\sigma'(z_h))W_h$ in residual layers $h\ge2$. Within the stated ball, $\|W_h\|\le(B_w+D/\sqrt m)\sqrt m$. Products of consecutive $P_h$, $h\ge2$, therefore have norm at most $A^H$ in the fully connected case and $\prod_h(1+C/H)\le e^C$ in the residual case. All estimates below use only $h\ge2$ for matrix operator norms; the input is fixed. [F1, F2, given, algebra, F6]

3.1 For a unit parameter direction $v$, let $\xi_h=D x_h[v]$. At the first layer $\|\xi_1\|\le C\|v_{W_1}\|/\sqrt m$. Subsequent layers obey $\xi_h=P_h\xi_{h-1}+(s_h/\sqrt m)\operatorname{diag}(\sigma'(z_h))v_{W_h}x_{h-1}$. The product bounds in step 1.1, the feature bounds in step 2.1, and Cauchy–Schwarz over layer blocks give $\max_h\|\xi_h\|\le T/\sqrt m$ or $C/\sqrt m$. For the residual case use $\sum_{h\ge2}s_h\|v_{W_h}\|\le c_{\rm res}(\sum_{h\ge2}\|v_{W_h}\|^2)^{1/2}/\sqrt H\le C$, retaining the separate first-layer term. Thus $\|D z_h[v]\|\le T$ or $C$, uniformly in $h$. Since $Df_i[v]=v_a^Tx_H+a^T\xi_H$ and $\|a\|\le C\sqrt m$, each output gradient has norm at most $T$ or $C$, proving $\|J\|\le T\sqrt n$ or $C\sqrt n$. 3.3 For the last-hidden-layer Gram, put $X_i=x_i^{(H-1)}$, $Z_i=W_HX_i$ and $\gamma=c_\sigma$ or $c_{\rm res}^2/H^2$. Direct differentiation gives $G_{H,ij}=\gamma\langle X_i,X_j\rangle m^{-1}\sum_ra_r^2\sigma'(Z_{i,r})\sigma'(Z_{j,r})$. 4.1 For two unit parameter directions $v,w$, twice differentiating the output gives the mixed output-weight terms $v_a^TDx_H[w]+w_a^TDx_H[v]$, and the sum over layers of $\frac{s_h}{\sqrt m}b_h^T\left(\operatorname{diag}(\sigma''(z_h))(Dz_h[v]\odot Dz_h[w])+\operatorname{diag}(\sigma'(z_h))(v_{W_h}Dx_{h-1}[w]+w_{W_h}Dx_{h-1}[v])\right).$ This identity follows by differentiating every primitive twice and propagating each resulting second-order term through its downstream Jacobians; the linear skip has zero second derivative. [F1, F2, step 3.1, step 3.2, algebra]

source_paragraphs.quote: 3.1 Write $\widehat S_{ij}^{(h)}=\langle x_i^{(h)}(0),x_j^{(h)}(0)\rangle$ and, for residual layers, $\widehat b_i^{(h)}=m^{-1/2}\sum_r x_{i,r}^{(h)}(0)$. Conditional on previous layers, the preactivation pairs in distinct rows are independent centered Gaussians with covariance given by $\widehat S^{(h-1)}$. In the fully connected case, step 1.1 bounds each difference of $\widehat S_{ij}^{(h)}$ from its conditional mean by $Ct_0$, except with probability $\delta/(32Hn^2)$, where $t_0=\sqrt{\log(64Hn^2/\delta)/m}$. Its conditional mean is exactly the fully connected population expectation evaluated at $\widehat S^{(h-1)}$. Since the population diagonal is one, step 2.1 gives, while the error is at most a fixed small constant, $e_h\le C e_{h-1}+Ct_0$, where $e_h=\max_{ij}|\widehat S_{ij}^{(h)}-K_{ij}^{(h)}|$ and $e_0=0$. If $B>1$ is a fixed base for this recurrence, then $e_h\le B^Ht_0$ after enlarging its prefactor. Choose the statement constant $A\ge B^2$ and enlarge the width constant; its term $Tn^2\log(16Hn/\delta)/\lambda^2$, with $T=A^H$, then makes this error smaller than both the fixed stopping threshold and $c\lambda/n$. Conditional bounds and a union bound over $h,i,j$ therefore justify the estimates through layers $h<H$; the last hidden-feature norm is bounded by one further conditional application of the activation moment estimate, without identifying its covariance with the terminal derivative kernel. A first layer crossing the stopping threshold would contradict this recurrence. In particular all feature norms are bounded by a constant, hence by $T$. [F1, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

5.1 For either architecture, conditional on layers before the last, the last-hidden-layer Jacobian Gram entries are $s_H^2\widehat S_{ij}^{(H-1)}m^{-1}\sum_ra_r^2\sigma'(z_{i,r})\sigma'(z_{j,r})$, where $s_H^2=c_\sigma$ for the fully connected case and $s_H^2=c_{\rm res}^2/H^2$ for residual $H\ge2$. Steps 1.1–2.1, the feature bounds and errors just proved give entry error at most $B_2^Ht_0$ in the fully connected case, for a fixed base $B_2$ depending only on the fixed activation bounds, and at most $Ct_0/H^2$ in the residual case. Choose the statement constant $A$ also with $A\ge B_2^2$; the displayed logarithmic width term and a sufficiently large fixed multiplier then make both errors at most $\lambda/(4n)$. If an $n\times n$ matrix $E$ has entries bounded by $\varepsilon$, then for any $z$, $\|Ez\|_2\le\sqrt n\,\varepsilon\sum_j|z_j|\le n\varepsilon\|z\|_2$ by [F6], hence $\|E\|_{\rm op}\le n\varepsilon$. source_paragraphs.quote: 1.1 Fix all vectors except $Y_{n,j}$. Replacing that vector by another vector $Y'_{n,j}$ changes $B_n$ by removing $Y_{n,j}Y_{n,j}^{\mathsf T}$ and adding $Y'_{n,j}(Y'_{n,j})^{\mathsf T}$. Applying [F1] once to remove the first term and once to add the second shows that $\operatorname{tr}(B_n-zI)^{-1}$ changes by at most $2/\eta$. Hence each of the real and imaginary parts of $M_n(z)$ has coordinate oscillation at most $c_j=2/(d_n\eta)$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Apply [F2] separately to $\operatorname{Re}M_n(z)$ and $\operatorname{Im}M_n(z)$. If a complex number has modulus greater than $t$, at least one of its real or imaginary parts has magnitude greater than $t/\sqrt2$. The union bound therefore gives $$\Pr\{|M_n(z)-\mathbb E M_n(z)|>t\} \le4\exp\left(-\frac{t^2d_n^2\eta^2}{4n}\right).$$ This is the stated estimate. [A1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

32.1 At $a=0$, the quotient is the polynomial obtained by canceling the factor $x$, so there is no singularity to interpret. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 31.1]

34.1 Choose $\max(a,L)<t<u<b$. The positive contribution from $[t,u]$ is at least $t^q(t-L)\int_t^u w(x)dx$. Since $t>L$ and $w>0$ on $(a,b)$, $I_q>0$ for some finite integer $q$ (and for all sufficiently large $q$). If $L\le a$, positivity follows directly. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 33.1]

40.1 Because $B-u>B-U>0$ and the positive interval has positive integral, $J_q>0$ for some finite integer $q$. The positive limiting trace excludes this for every sufficiently large $n$. Hence $\lambda_{\min}^{+}(S_n)<U$ eventually. Let $U\downarrow a$ through a countable sequence to obtain $\limsup\lambda_{\min}^{+}\le a$. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 39.1]

41.1 For $\gamma=1$, $a=0$. The same argument chooses $0<t<u<U$ and proves an eventually positive eigenvalue below every prescribed $U>0$. The factor $x$ removes every exact zero eigenvalue, including arbitrary extra rank defects, so no rank theorem or lower-rank estimate is concealed in this case. Since eigenvalues are nonnegative, this also proves $\lambda_{\min}^{+}\to0$ in the square-aspect-ratio case. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 40.1] ∎

anchor: Proof step 1.1 (the finite diagonal/off-diagonal variance expansion and its coefficient maximum)

source_paragraphs.quote: 1.1 First fix a deterministic complex symmetric matrix $A$. Since $A_{ji}=A_{ij}$, $$\xi^{\mathsf T}A\xi-\operatorname{tr}A =\sum_i A_{ii}(\xi_i^2-1)+2\sum_{i<j}A_{ij}\xi_i\xi_j.$$ The diagonal summands have mean zero. Distinct diagonal summands are uncorrelated; a diagonal summand and an off-diagonal summand are uncorrelated because at least one independent centered coordinate occurs to the first power; and two off-diagonal summands are uncorrelated unless their unordered index pairs coincide. Therefore $$\mathbb E\left|\xi^{\mathsf T}A\xi-\operatorname{tr}A\right|^2 =(\mu_4-1)\sum_i|A_{ii}|^2+4\sum_{i<j}|A_{ij}|^2 \le C_{\mu_4}\sum_{i,j}|A_{ij}|^2.$$ Here $\mu_4\ge1$ follows from $\mathbb E\xi_i^2=1$ and Cauchy–Schwarz. [given, F1, algebra]

source_paragraphs.quote: 1.1 Put $B=2\sqrt\gamma$, $A_0=1+\gamma$, and $x(\theta)=A_0+B\cos\theta$ for $0<\theta<\pi$. This substitution maps $(0,\pi)$ onto $(a,b)$ in reverse order, with $\sqrt{(b-x)(x-a)}=B\sin\theta$ and $|dx|=B\sin\theta\,d\theta$. Thus the continuous part of $\mu_\gamma$ becomes $(2/\pi)\sin^2\theta\,d\theta/x(\theta)$. For real $A>B$, the substitution $t=\tan(\theta/2)$ gives $$\int_0^\pi\frac{d\theta}{A+B\cos\theta}=2\int_0^\infty\frac{dt}{(A+B)+(A-B)t^2}=\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{A^2-B^2}}.$$ Write $I_0(A)=\int_0^\pi(A+B\cos\theta)^{-1}d\theta=\pi/\sqrt{A^2-B^2}$. Since $\int_0^\pi\cos\theta\,d\theta=0$ and $\cos\theta/(A+B\cos\theta)=B^{-1}-A/[B(A+B\cos\theta)]$, $$I_1(A):=\int_0^\pi\frac{\cos\theta}{A+B\cos\theta}d\theta=\frac\pi B-\frac A B I_0(A),\quad I_2(A):=\int_0^\pi\frac{\cos^2\theta}{A+B\cos\theta}d\theta=-\frac A B I_1(A)=-\frac{A\pi}{B^2}+\frac{A^2}{B^2}I_0(A).$$ Therefore $$J(A):=\int_0^\pi\frac{\sin^2\theta}{A+B\cos\theta}\,d\theta=I_0(A)-I_2(A)=\frac{\pi(A-\sqrt{A^2-B^2})}{B^2}.$$ For $A=A_0>B$, the root is $|1-\gamma|$; if $\gamma=1$, direct cancellation $\sin^2\theta/(2+2\cos\theta)= (1-\cos\theta)/2$ gives the same value by continuity. Hence the continuous mass is $2J(A_0)/\pi=(A_0-|1-\gamma|)/(2\gamma)=\min(1,\gamma)/\gamma$. Adding $(1-1/\gamma)_+$ gives total mass one. Define $f_\gamma(x):=\sqrt{(b-x)(x-a)}/(2\pi\gamma x)$ for $a<x<b$ and $f_\gamma(x):=0$ otherwise. This is nonnegative and Borel measurable, and has finite integral by the calculation above. By [F4], $A\mapsto\int_A f_\gamma\,d\lambda$ is a finite Borel measure; the nonnegative multiple $(1-1/\gamma)_+\delta_0$ is a finite measure as well. Their sum is the displayed set function, so it is a Borel probability measure supported on $[0,\infty)$. [F1, F4, algebra, construct]

source_paragraphs.quote: 1.1 Apply F1 to the original nested rectangular array and, as necessary, its transpose. Orient the centered truncated matrix with $p$ rows and $n$ columns, $p\le n$, and divide by $\sqrt n$. In this proof the original sequence index is $h$, $n=N_h=\max(h,p_h)$, $p=\min(h,p_h)$, and $y_n=p/n\to y\in(0,1]$. These dimensions are comparable to $h$; all probability series below are summed over $h$. Enlarge the slow truncation threshold by a fixed factor to bound the centered entries by $L_n=\delta_n\sqrt n$ with $\delta_n\ge1/\log(n+2)$, $\delta_n\to0$. F1 gives independent centered entries, variance at most one, and $E|x|^q\le CL_n^{q-3}$ for $q\ge3$. Define $Y=(x_{ij}/\sqrt n)$ and the restricted matrices $T_\ell$ as in the statement. The same arguments hold if the orientation changes infinitely often. [F1, given, construct]

2.1 Fix $\ell\ge1$. Set $N=4m\ell$, with integer $m$ chosen so that $m/\log n\to\infty$ and $\delta_n(m/\log n)^2\to0$; for example $m=\lceil\log n\,\delta_n^{-1/8}\rceil$. Since $\delta_n\ge1/\log n$, $N$ is polylogarithmic. Reversing each admissible path exchanges its endpoints and preserves its real weight, so $T_\ell$ is real symmetric. Thus its even-power trace bounds $\|T_\ell\|^{2m}$. Expand $E\operatorname{tr}T_\ell^{2m}$ into closed alternating walks of length $N$, split into $2m$ consecutive nonbacktracking blocks of length $2\ell$. Bound absolute expectations termwise. Any edge appearing exactly once vanishes by centering and independence. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

7.1 Given innovation and T3 positions, choose the $t$ T4 edge classes in at most $(k+1)^{2t}$ ways and assign all T4 positions to classes in at most $t^d$ ways. Innovation endpoints are forced by canonical order. At any T3 position there are at most $2t+1$ choices, and at most $d$ positions can be regular. A decision tree of depth at most $d$ with branching at most $2t+1$ has at most $(2t+1)^d$ leaves (pad shorter branches with forced dummy choices); no separate selection of regular positions is required. T4 endpoints are forced by current vertex and chosen class, or the code is invalid. Thus the remaining coding factor is at most $(k+1)^{2t}t^d(2t+1)^d\le(k+1)^{2t}3^d(t+1)^{2d}$. Interpret $0^0=1$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra, step 6.1]

10.1 Combining all factors, with $A=(2\ell+1)(\ell+1)$, gives $$E\operatorname{tr}T_\ell^{2m}\le nA^{2m}y_n^{-m}\sum_{1\le k\le N/2}\binom{N-k}{k}y_n^{k/2}\delta_n^{N-2k}3^{N-2k}\sum_{t=0}^{N-2k}q_{n,k}^{t}(t+1)^{2(N-2k)},$$ where $q_{n,k}=C(2\ell+1)^2(k+1)^2/(\sqrt{ny_n}\delta_n)$. This derivation uses absolute values and requires no symmetry of the real entry law. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra, step 9.1]

11.1 For real $|t|\ge1+\epsilon$, write $|t|=\cosh a$ and $\rho=e^a>1$. The recurrence directly gives $U_j(\cosh a)=\sinh((j+1)a)/\sinh a$ and $U_j(-t)=(-1)^jU_j(t)$. Hence $|U_j(t)|\ge\rho^j$ and $|U_{j-1}(t)|/|U_j(t)|\le\rho^{-1}$, the last inequality following from $\sinh(ja)/\sinh((j+1)a)<e^{-a}$. Therefore $|U_j(t)+\sqrt yU_{j-1}(t)|\ge(1-\sqrt y/\rho)\rho^j\ge(1-\rho^{-1})\rho^j$. This is strictly positive uniformly for $|t|\ge1+\epsilon$, including $y=1$. source_paragraphs.quote: 1.1 For $\eta>0$, the imaginary part of the integrand in [F1] is $\eta/((x-u)^2+\eta^2)$. For each $x\in\mathbb R$, $$\int_a^b\frac{\eta}{(x-u)^2+\eta^2}\,du=\arctan\frac{b-x}{\eta}-\arctan\frac{a-x}{\eta}\le\pi.$$ Lebesgue measure restricted to $[a,b]$ and the probability measure $\mu$ are sigma-finite. Tonelli [F5] shows that the nonnegative product integrand has integral at most $\pi\mu(\mathbb R)=\pi$, so it belongs to $L^1$ on the product space. Fubini [F2] therefore gives $$\frac1\pi\int_a^b\operatorname{Im}m_\mu(u+i\eta)\,du=\int K_{\eta,a,b}(x)\,d\mu(x),\quad K_{\eta,a,b}(x)=\frac1\pi\left(\arctan\frac{b-x}{\eta}-\arctan\frac{a-x}{\eta}\right).$$ The kernel lies in $[0,1]$ and tends pointwise to $1$ on $(a,b)$, $1/2$ at either endpoint, and $0$ elsewhere. [F3] gives the interval formula in the Statement, including endpoint atoms. [F1, F2, F3, F5, given, algebra]

1.2 For any $x\in\mathbb R$, $$\eta\operatorname{Im}m_\mu(x+i\eta)=\int\frac{\eta^2}{(t-x)^2+\eta^2}\,d\mu(t).$$ The integrand is bounded by $1$ and tends to $\mathbf1_{\{x\}}(t)$ as $\eta\downarrow0$. Dominated convergence [F3] proves the atom formula. [F1, F3, algebra]

3.1 The family $\mathcal P=\{\varnothing,\mathbb R\}\cup\{(a,b):a<b\}$ is a pi-system: the intersection of two open intervals is another open interval or empty. It generates the Borel sigma-algebra because open intervals form a basis. The class of Borel sets on which $\mu$ and $\nu$ agree is a lambda-system: it contains $\mathbb R$ because both measures are probabilities, is closed under complements by finite total mass, and is closed under disjoint countable unions by countable additivity. Step 2.1 and [F4] therefore give equality on every Borel set, so $\mu=\nu$. [F4, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

source_paragraphs.quote: 2.1 Set $\psi=v(e^{ty}-1-ty)/y^2\ge0$. Independence shows that $M_k=\exp(t\sum_{j\le k}W_j-k\psi)$ has conditional expected next value at most $M_k$. If $\tau$ is the first $k\le N$ with $\sum_{j\le k}W_j\ge x$, stopping this finite sequence at $\tau$ or $N$ preserves the expectation bound $1$: condition each increment and observe that the indicator of not having stopped is determined by the preceding variables. On a crossing its stopped value is at least $e^{tx-N\psi}$. Nonnegativity therefore gives $P(\max_{k\le N}\sum_{j\le k}W_j\ge x)\le e^{-tx+N\psi}$. This proves the needed maximal bound directly. [step 1.1, algebra]

source_paragraphs.quote: 1.1 Fix $z=u+i\eta$ with $\eta>0$. Write the transpose of row $i$ of $X_n$ as $y_i\in\mathbb R^{p_n}$ and set $Q=(S_n-zI)^{-1}$, $m_n=p_n^{-1}\operatorname{tr}Q=m_{\mu_n}(z)$ by [F1] and [F2]. For each $i$, let $S_i=S_n-y_iy_i^{\mathsf T}/n$, $Q_i=(S_i-zI)^{-1}$ and $\beta_i=n^{-1}y_i^{\mathsf T}Q_i y_i$. The matrices $S_n,S_i$ are nonnegative symmetric, so their resolvents exist; diagonalizing $S_i$ expresses $\beta_i$ as a sum of nonnegative weights times $(\lambda-z)^{-1}$ with $\lambda\ge0$. Thus $\operatorname{Im}\beta_i\ge0$ and $\operatorname{Im}(z\beta_i)\ge0$, since $\operatorname{Im}[z/(\lambda-z)]=\eta\lambda/|\lambda-z|^2\ge0$. Consequently $\operatorname{Im}[z(1+\beta_i)]\ge\eta$, so $|1+\beta_i|\ge\eta/|z|>0$. Applying [F4] with $x=y_i/\sqrt n$ gives $Q=Q_i-Q_i y_i y_i^{\mathsf T}Q_i/[n(1+\beta_i)]$, so $n^{-1}y_i^{\mathsf T}Qy_i=\beta_i/(1+\beta_i)$. Since $S_nQ=I+zQ$, taking normalized traces yields $$1+z m_n=\frac1{p_n}\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{\beta_i}{1+\beta_i}.$$ [given, F1, F2, F4, algebra]

4.1 The sequence $(a_n)$ is bounded by $1/\eta$. Moreover $\operatorname{Im}(z m_n)=p_n^{-1}\sum_j\eta\lambda_j(S_n)/|\lambda_j(S_n)-z|^2\ge0$, so $\operatorname{Im}(1-\gamma_n-z-\gamma_n z a_n)\le-\eta$. The same closed-cone bound gives $|1+\gamma_na_n|\ge\eta/|z|$. Every convergent subsequence of $a_n$ therefore has a limit $a$, with $|1+\gamma a|\ge\eta/|z|$, satisfying $1+za=a/(1+\gamma a)$ and $\operatorname{Im}(1-\gamma-z-\gamma za)\le-\eta$. The two roots of the associated quadratic have corresponding values $D_j=1-\gamma-z-\gamma z a_j$ whose sum is $1-\gamma-z$, with imaginary part $-\eta$. Thus at most one root can have $\operatorname{Im}D_j\le-\eta$. By [F6], that root is $m_\gamma(z)$. All subsequential limits are consequently $m_\gamma(z)$, so $a_n\to m_\gamma(z)$ and step 3.1 gives $m_n(z)\to m_\gamma(z)$ almost surely. [F1, F6, step 3.1, algebra]

6.1 On this probability-one event, $\int x\,d\mu_n(x)=T_n$ and $\mu_n$ is supported on $[0,\infty)$ by [F1]. For every $R>0$, $\mu_n((R,\infty))\le T_n/R$, so the sequence is tight. By [A1] and [F8], every subsequence has a further weakly convergent subsequence with limit $
u$. Along it, [F11] applied to $x\mapsto(x-z)^{-1}$ shows $m_
u(z)=m_\gamma(z)$ on the dense set from step 5.1. The transforms are continuous because $|m_
u(z)-m_
u(w)|\le|z-w|/(\operatorname{Im}z\operatorname{Im}w)$ for $z,w\in\mathbb C^+$; equality therefore extends to all $z\in\mathbb C^+$. [F1, F8, F11, step 5.1, A1, algebra]

source_paragraphs.quote: 7.1 By [F7], every weak subsequential limit $\nu$ in step 6.1 equals $\mu_\gamma$. If $\mu_n$ did not converge weakly to $\mu_\gamma$, some bounded continuous test function and a subsequence would have integrals separated from its $\mu_\gamma$ integral by a fixed positive amount; tightness would give a further weakly convergent subsequence, contradicting its limit $\mu_\gamma$. Therefore $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu_\gamma$ almost surely. [F7, F8, F11, step 6.1, algebra] ∎

source_paragraphs.quote: 1.1 Put $P_{\ker X_n}=I_{p_n}-X_n^+X_n$. For any fixed $v\in\mathbb R^{p_n}$, $\mathbb E_{z_{0,n}}(z_{0,n}^{\mathsf T}v)^2=v^{\mathsf T}\mathbb E[z_{0,n}z_{0,n}^{\mathsf T}]v=\|v\|_2^2$, so the stated prediction risk equals $\mathbb E_{\varepsilon_n}[\|\widehat\beta_n-\beta_n\|_2^2\mid X_n]$. By [F2], $P_n:=X_n^+X_n$ is an orthogonal projection. The Penrose equation $X_nX_n^+X_n=X_n$ shows $\ker(P_n)=\ker(X_n)$: if $X_nv=0$, then $P_nv=0$, and if $P_nv=0$, then $X_nv=X_nX_n^+X_nv=X_nP_nv=0$. Hence $\operatorname{Ran}(P_n)=\ker(X_n)^\perp=\operatorname{Ran}(X_n^{\mathsf T})$ by the right-singular-vector basis in [F3], so $\widehat\beta_n-\beta_n=-P_{\ker X_n}\beta_n+X_n^+\varepsilon_n$. Conditional on $X_n$, the cross term has expectation zero because $\mathbb E[\varepsilon_n\mid X_n]=0$. Its noise contribution is $$\mathbb E_{\varepsilon_n}\|X_n^+\varepsilon_n\|_2^2=\sigma^2\operatorname{tr}(X_n^+(X_n^+)^{\mathsf T})=\sigma^2\operatorname{tr}((X_n^{\mathsf T}X_n)^+)=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\operatorname{tr}(S_n^+),$$ where the middle equality follows by writing an SVD and the last uses $(aB)^+=a^{-1}B^+$ for $a>0$. With $x_n=\beta_n/r$, this proves the exact identity $$\mathcal R_n=r^2x_n^{\mathsf T}P_{\ker X_n}x_n+\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\operatorname{tr}(S_n^+).$$ [given, A2, A3, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Suppose $\gamma<1$ and set $a=(1-\sqrt\gamma)^2>0$. By [F4], $X_n$ has full column rank eventually and every eigenvalue of $S_n$ is at least $a/2$ eventually. Thus the bias term in step 1.1 is zero and $p_n^{-1}\operatorname{tr}(S_n^+)=\int f(t)d\mu_n(t)$ for the bounded continuous function $f(t)=1/\max(t,a/2)$. By [F5] and [F8], this converges to $J_\gamma=\int t^{-1}d\mu_\gamma(t)$, since the Marchenko–Pastur support is bounded below by $a$. For $s>0$, define $m_\gamma(-s)=\int(t+s)^{-1}d\mu_\gamma(t)$. The integrands are bounded by $1/a$ and converge pointwise to $1/t$, so [F10] gives $m_\gamma(-s)\to J_\gamma$ as $s\downarrow0$. The fixed-point equation in [F7], initially stated for $z\in\mathbb C^+$, extends to $z=-s<0$ by dominated convergence in its defining integral; its denominator stays nonzero because $1+\gamma m_\gamma(-s)>0$. Taking $s\downarrow0$ yields $1+(\gamma-1)J_\gamma=0$, hence $J_\gamma=1/(1-\gamma)$. Since $p_n/n\to\gamma$, step 1.1 gives $\mathcal R_n\to\sigma^2\gamma/(1-\gamma)$. [given, A1, F4, F5, F7, F8, F10, F11, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Suppose $\gamma>1$ and set $a=(\sqrt\gamma-1)^2>0$. By [F4], $X_n$ has full row rank eventually, $S_n$ has exactly $p_n-n$ zero eigenvalues, and all positive eigenvalues are at least $a/2$ eventually. The continuous function $g(t)=\max(1-2t/a,0)$ equals one at zero and vanishes on the positive spectrum for all sufficiently large $n$. Hence $x_n^{\mathsf T}P_{\ker X_n}x_n=\int g(t)d\mu_n^{x_n}(t)\to\int g(t)dF_{\gamma,\delta_1}(t)=1-1/\gamma$ by [F6], [F7], and [F9]; [F9] identifies the limit with $\mu_\gamma$, on whose positive support $g=0$ and whose zero atom has mass $1-1/\gamma$. Define $h(0)=0$ and, for $t>0$, $h(t)=t^{-1}\min(1,\max(0,4t/a-1))$. This is bounded and continuous, equals zero at zero, and equals $1/t$ for $t\ge a/2$. Therefore $p_n^{-1}\operatorname{tr}(S_n^+)=\int h(t)d\mu_n(t)\to J_\gamma^+:=\int_{(0,\infty)}t^{-1}d\mu_\gamma(t)$ by [F5] and [F8]. [F7] gives $m_\gamma(-s)=(1-1/\gamma)/s+J_\gamma^++o(1)$ as $s\downarrow0$: subtract the zero atom and use [F10] by dominated convergence on the positive support, whose lower endpoint is $a>0$. To compute the constant term, write $\alpha=1-1/\gamma$ and substitute $m=\alpha/s+J_\gamma^++o(1)$ into $1+(\gamma-1-s)m-\gamma s m^2=0$, the fixed-point equation at $z=-s$ (again obtained by dominated convergence from [F7]). The coefficient of $s^{-1}$ vanishes because $\gamma\alpha=\gamma-1$; the constant term is $1-\alpha-(\gamma-1)J_\gamma^++o(1)$. It must vanish, so $J_\gamma^+=1/[\gamma(\gamma-1)]$. Using $p_n/n\to\gamma$ in step 1.1 proves $\mathcal R_n\to r^2(1-1/\gamma)+\sigma^2/(\gamma-1)$. [given, A1, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, F9, F10, F11, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

anchor: Proof step 1.1 (compact norm-attaining unit vectors and finite sphere nets with a packing bound)

source_paragraphs.quote: 1.1 If $K=0$, every entry is zero almost surely and the conclusion is immediate. Assume $K>0$. Regard the complex unit sphere in $\mathbb C^d$ as the real unit sphere in $\mathbb R^{2d}$. For $0<\varepsilon<1/2$, a maximal $\varepsilon$-separated subset is an $\varepsilon$-net; the disjoint radius-$\varepsilon/2$ balls about its points lie in the radius-$(1+\varepsilon/2)$ ball, so volume comparison bounds its cardinality by $(1+2/\varepsilon)^{2d}$. If $\mathcal N_1,\mathcal N_2$ are such nets for the two unit spheres and $A$ is an $n\times N$ complex matrix, approximating unit vectors $u,v$ attaining $\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}=|u^*Av|$ gives $$\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le (1-2\varepsilon)^{-1}\max_{u_0\in\mathcal N_1,\ v_0\in\mathcal N_2}|u_0^*Av_0|.$$ Indeed, the approximation error is at most $\|u-u_0\|\|A\|+\|v-v_0\|\|A\|\le2\varepsilon\|A\|$. [given, F4, algebra]

anchor: Proof steps 2.1 and 3.1 (the nonzero rank-one denominator and finite-product column averages)

source_paragraphs.quote: 2.1 Write $s_{n,j}=T_n^{1/2}X_{n,\cdot j}/\sqrt{N_n}$, $A_{n,j}=A_n-s_{n,j}s_{n,j}^*$, and $R_{n,j}=(A_{n,j}-zI)^{-1}$. By [F4], $$U_{n,j}:=x_n^*(R_n-R_{n,j})x_n=-\frac{(x_n^*R_{n,j}s_{n,j})(s_{n,j}^*R_{n,j}x_n)}{1+s_{n,j}^*R_{n,j}s_{n,j}}.$$ Diagonalizing $A_{n,j}$ as in [F6] gives $\operatorname{Im}(z(1+s_{n,j}^*R_{n,j}s_{n,j}))\ge\eta$, hence the denominator has modulus at least $\eta/|z|$. Conditional on all columns except $j$, each factor in the numerator is a linear form in the bounded independent entries of column $j$, with coefficient-vector norm at most $\sqrt M/(\eta\sqrt{N_n})$. Step 1.1 and Cauchy–Schwarz therefore give $\mathbb E|U_{n,j}|^4\le C N_n^{-4}$. [given, F2, F4, F6, F8, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $\mathcal F_{n,j}=\sigma(X_{n,\cdot1},\ldots,X_{n,\cdot j})$, and let $E_{n,j}$ be the finite-product average over the remaining columns. By [F2]–[F3], $$x_n^*R_nx_n-\mathbb E[x_n^*R_nx_n]=\sum_{j=1}^{N_n}(E_{n,j}-E_{n,j-1})x_n^*R_nx_n.$$ The leave-one-column resolvent $R_{n,j}$ depends on all columns except $j$, so its product-integral averages under $E_{n,j}$ and $E_{n,j-1}$ agree. Therefore the $j$th summand is $D_{n,j}:=(E_{n,j}-E_{n,j-1})U_{n,j}$. Integrating over column $j$ shows $E_{n,j-1}D_{n,j}=0$, so these are martingale differences. Conditional Jensen gives $\mathbb E|D_{n,j}|^4\le16\mathbb E|U_{n,j}|^4\le C N_n^{-4}$. [given, F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra]

source_paragraphs.quote: 1.1 Write $\kappa_n=N_n/n\to1/c$, $\sigma_R^2=\mathbb E(\operatorname{Re}\xi_{11})^2$, and $\sigma_I^2=\mathbb E(\operatorname{Im}\xi_{11})^2$. Centering of $\xi_{11}$ makes both real coordinates centered, and $\sigma_R^2+\sigma_I^2=\tau^2$. If $\sigma_R>0$, the matrices $Z_n=\operatorname{Re}X_n/\sigma_R$ are upper-left blocks of one real iid array with mean zero, variance one and finite fourth moment. Applying [F2] with $\gamma=\kappa=1/c$ and then [F3] gives $$\limsup_n\frac{\|\operatorname{Re}X_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}}{\sqrt{N_n}}\le\sigma_R\frac{1+\sqrt\kappa}{\sqrt\kappa}=\sigma_R(1+\sqrt c)\quad\text{almost surely}.$$ If $\sigma_R=0$, the centered real part is zero almost surely, so the same bound holds. The identical argument for the imaginary part gives the bound with $\sigma_I$. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 The complex operator norm satisfies $\|X_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\|\operatorname{Re}X_n+i\operatorname{Im}X_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\|\operatorname{Re}X_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|\operatorname{Im}X_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}$. Intersecting the two probability-one events from step 1.1 proves the asserted limsup bound. Finally, $\sigma_R+\sigma_I\le\sqrt{2(\sigma_R^2+\sigma_I^2)}=\sqrt2\tau$ by Cauchy–Schwarz, giving the unit-variance consequence. [given, F4, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

source_paragraphs.quote: 1.1 Let $\xi$ have the common entry law. For integer $K$, set $\xi^{(K)}=\xi\mathbf1_{\{|\xi|\le K\}}-\mathbb E[\xi\mathbf1_{\{|\xi|\le K\}}]$, $\sigma_K^2=\mathbb E|\xi^{(K)}|^2$, and $\Delta^{(K)}=\xi-\xi^{(K)}$. Then $\sigma_K\to1$, and $\tau_K^2:=\mathbb E|\Delta^{(K)}|^2\to0$ because $\mathbb E\xi=0$ and $\mathbb E|\xi|^2<\infty$. For all sufficiently large $K$, $\sigma_K>0$; put $\zeta^{(K)}=\xi^{(K)}/\sigma_K$. These entries are centered, bounded, iid and have unit second absolute moment, while $\Delta^{(K)}$ is centered iid with finite fourth moment. At matrix level, $X_n=\sigma_K Z_n^{(K)}+D_n^{(K)}$, where $Z_n^{(K)}$ and $D_n^{(K)}$ are the common upper-left blocks formed from $\zeta^{(K)}$ and $\Delta^{(K)}$. [given, F1, F2, F7, algebra]

3.1 Fix $z\in\mathbb C^+$ and a deterministic unit direction sequence $x_n$. For each such $K$, [F1] applied to $Z_n^{(K)}$ gives $x_n^*(A_n^{(K)}-zI)^{-1}x_n\to m_{c,H}(z)$ almost surely, with the transform convention [F9]. By step 2.1, $$\limsup_n\left|x_n^*(A_n-zI)^{-1}x_n-m_{c,H}(z)\right|\le\frac{M C_c^2}{(\operatorname{Im}z)^2}\left((1+\sigma_K)\tau_K+|\sigma_K^2-1|\right)$$ on the probability-one event obtained by intersecting the events from step 2.1 with the almost-sure convergence event for this fixed truncation level. The right side tends to zero as $K\to\infty$, so the directional Stieltjes transforms converge almost surely at every fixed $z\in\mathbb C^+$. Intersecting over a countable dense set gives simultaneous convergence there. [given, F1, F9, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 By [F2], $\|A_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le M\|X_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2/N_n$ is almost surely eventually bounded. Thus the directional laws are eventually supported on one compact interval; [F3] makes them probability measures and [F8] gives their exact spectral-measure meaning. They are therefore tight. The half-line is Polish: it is closed in the complete real line and has dense subset $\mathbb Q\cap[0,\infty)$, as required by [F6]. By [A1] and [F4], each subsequence has a weakly convergent further subsequence. Its transform equals $m_{c,H}$ on the dense set by step 3.1; continuity of Stieltjes transforms extends equality to $\mathbb C^+$, and [F5] identifies the subsequential limit as $F_{c,H}$. The bounded-continuous-test definition [F10] yields the stated weak convergence. Every subsequence has the same further limit, proving the asserted almost-sure limit. [given, A1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F8, F10, F11, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

Therefore every subsequence has the same further limit, which by the bounded-continuous-test definition [F12] proves $\mu_n^{x_n}\Rightarrow F_{c,H}$ almost surely. source_paragraphs.quote: 1.1 Regard the network as a finite composition of $C^1$ maps on its Euclidean parameter space; [F1] gives the shared-parameter gradients. Let $J_f(\theta(t))$ be the Jacobian of $(f_\theta(x_i))_{i=1}^N$. It is continuous in $\theta$ because $\sigma$ is $C^2$, and it is bounded on the compact image of the continuous path $\theta([0,T])$. The flow equation and $d\in L^1([0,T];\mathbb R^N)$ therefore imply $\dot\theta\in L^1([0,T])$. By [F8], applied to each of the finitely many parameter coordinates, $\theta$ is absolutely continuous and its increments equal the integrals of its derivative. Define the terminal array by $D^L_{1i}(t)=d_i(t)$, and obtain each hidden backpropagated array $D^{\ell+1}(t)\in\mathbb R^{n_{\ell+1}\times N}$ by weighting the derivative of each data-point output with $d_i(t)$. If $Z^\ell(t)\in\mathbb R^{n_\ell\times N}$ is the activation array, the weight and bias equations are $\dot W^{(\ell)}=-D^{\ell+1}(Z^\ell)^T/(N\sqrt{n_\ell})$ and $\dot b^{(\ell)}=-\beta D^{\ell+1}\mathbf1/N$, while hidden backpropagation is $D^\ell=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma\prime(U^\ell))(W^{(\ell)})^TD^{\ell+1}/\sqrt{n_\ell}$. Here division by $N$ acts on the data sum. [A1, F1, F3, F8, given, algebra]

6.1 For each layer, the exact tangent-kernel block recursion is $K^{\ell+1}_{(i,c),(j,d)}=\delta_{cd}(n_\ell^{-1}\sum_a Z^\ell_{ai}Z^\ell_{aj}+\beta^2)+n_\ell^{-1}\sum_{a,b}W^{(\ell)}_{ca}W^{(\ell)}_{db}\sigma'(U^\ell_{ai})\sigma'(U^\ell_{bj})K^\ell_{(i,a),(j,b)}$. It follows by applying the chain rule to each coordinate and splitting parameter derivatives into the current layer and earlier shared parameters, as in [F1]. The first term varies uniformly by the activation and hidden-bias estimates in step 5.1. For the second term, for each output index $c$ and data index $i$ use the vector $v_{c,i}(t)\in\mathbb R^{n_\ell}$ with entries $W^{(\ell)}_{ca}(t)\sigma'(U^\ell_{ai}(t))$. Their normalized Euclidean norms stay bounded. Their changes tend to zero in normalized Euclidean norm: the weight-change part is bounded by $c\|\Delta W_c\|_2/\sqrt{n_\ell}$, while Cauchy–Schwarz for the initial-weight part gives $n_\ell^{-1}\sum_a|W^{(\ell)}_{ca}(0)|^2|\Delta\sigma'_{ai}|^2\le(n_\ell^{-1}\sum_a|W^{(\ell)}_{ca}(0)|^4)^{1/2}(n_\ell^{-1}\sum_a|\Delta\sigma'_{ai}|^4)^{1/2}$. The first factor is stochastically bounded by [F3]–[F4]; the second tends uniformly to zero because [F7] gives $|\Delta\sigma'|\le M_2|\Delta U|$ and $|\Delta\sigma'|\le2c$, hence $|\Delta\sigma'|^4\le(2c)^2M_2^2|\Delta U|^2$; normalized preactivation changes tend to zero by step 5.1. For each fixed next-layer width, the finitely many output-index blocks have uniformly bounded subnetwork Gram operators by step 2.1, and induction from the constant first-layer Gram makes their changes tend uniformly to zero; applying $|\langle v,Kv'\rangle-\langle w,K_0w'\rangle|\le\|v-w\|\|K\|\|v'\|+\|w\|\|K-K_0\|\|v'\|+\|w\|\|K_0\|\|v'-w'\|$ at each of the finitely many layers proves uniform convergence of the finite-data kernel blocks. The output layer has fixed scalar dimension, so this is exactly $\sup_{t\le T}\|K_t-K_0\|_{op}\to0$ in probability. [F1, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, step 2.1, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

The parameter-flow equation and [F5] give $\dot f_t(x_i)=-N^{-1}\sum_jK_t(i,j)d_j(t)$. Integrating and subtracting the equation with $K_\infty$ yields $\sup_{t\le T}\|f_t-f_0+N^{-1}\int_0^tK_\infty d(s)\,ds\|_N\le N^{-1}\sup_{t\le T}\|K_t-K_\infty\|_{op}\int_0^T\|d(s)\|_Nds$.
